headline: Nothing about the game changed tonight. This was record keeping, plus one finding about our own tools that is worth knowing.
matters: Two things you asked for are now in place: the questions this lane needs you to answer are written out as real choices with costs, and finished work now publishes without asking you first. The finding is less comfortable. The way this editor describes how it finds the emulator looks like it was copied from another tool's documentation rather than measured against our own code, and that description has been handed to other lanes as fact for months. Nobody has checked it yet, and it is now written down as an open question instead of being quietly fixed.

headline: The editor was writing a background drift value the game could not read, and now it writes one it can. Every scene made in this editor carried it.
matters: When you set how far a background drifts up and down, the editor used to offer a list of named choices, and the name it started on was one the game reads as nonsense. The game did something that looked almost exactly like pinning the background still, with a one pixel wobble, which is why it went unnoticed. The setting is now a plain number box from 0 to 15, the saved test scenes that carried the bad value are corrected, and the scene built by hand in the editor was rebuilt in the editor rather than patched by hand. One thing is still unproven: nobody has watched the fix on real hardware or in the emulator, so what is certain is that we now write a value the game accepts, not yet that it looks right on screen.

headline: A moving background band built by hand in the editor now survives the whole trip into the engine's own tooling — and the test that was supposed to be checking this was broken.
matters: Until today the band path had only ever been proven with a band the code built for itself. Now one made the way an author would make it — typing the size, clicking Promote, pressing Ctrl+S — goes through the engine's own converter and comes out accepted, with the background picture pixel-for-pixel unchanged. The uncomfortable half: the check that judged this had a number typed into it that only matched one particular band size, so it called a perfectly correct result a failure, and would have done that for every band except the one it made itself. That is fixed and the fix is proven not to have made the check softer. Still not proven: none of this has been assembled into a ROM or run on the console, so the band has never actually moved on screen. Separately, the engine side has quietly fixed the thing that was blocking new bands: their art tool now keeps 128 tile slots back automatically. The existing background art has not been redone, so nothing is free yet, but the road you approved is now paved.

headline: Buttons in a panel's title bar no longer fold the panel shut when you click them.
matters: Adding a layer or deleting a scene used to also collapse the panel you were working in, so on an odd-numbered click the panel would slam shut on the thing you had just made — the heading would say eight layers over an empty box. That is fixed for every button in every panel title bar, including ones nobody has written yet, rather than patched on the two that were misbehaving. I checked it both ways on the merged code: with the fix every one of the thirty-one checks passes, and with the fix taken back out the exact failure you originally saw comes straight back. One thing I chose not to do: these panel headings still cannot be operated by keyboard at all, which is a separate and older problem, and I have written it down rather than quietly widening this fix into it.

headline: The editor was telling agents the wrong size limits for a level's background — one too generous, one too tight.
matters: A background picture has a hard ceiling on how many unique tiles it can use, set by where the console keeps its sprite table. The editor told agents that ceiling was higher than it really is, so an agent could build a background the console physically cannot hold and only find out later, at bake time or as garbage sprayed over the sprites. In the same breath it was too strict about height: it insisted every background be half the height the engine actually supports, which made a full-height background impossible to author through the agent path at all — even though backgrounds that size already exist in the library. Both numbers now come from the shared file that records what the engine really does, so the limit the editor enforces, the limit it advertises and the limit the engine holds are one number that cannot drift apart. Before this there was not a single test anywhere covering reading or writing a background through the agent path; there are now, and I checked them by breaking the code on purpose and confirming the right ones failed. The one thing left unproven is a full-height background making the whole trip through a real save and into the engine's own tooling — that needs the app running, so I have written it down rather than implying the tests covered it.
detail: ROADMAP item 8, merged 06bb119 (fix 1d0a770, first tests 258ebab, docs 18f0574, two more stale comments 1d7f4f1, count correction 484254d). Six sites; the gate with teeth was src/main/editor-methods.ts's zod .length(2048)/.max(512) in the MAIN process, one layer before the handler and never named in the row. Now derives BG_TILE_CAPACITY/BG_LAYOUT_WORDS/BG_LAYOUT_WORDS_LEGACY/LAYOUT_WORD_MAX/LAYOUT_TILE_INDEX_MASK/TILE_PIXELS/TILE_PIXEL_MAX from bganim-consumer-contract.json via bg-override.ts. get_bg measures height off the act's layout, null when absent. Height widening NOT blocked: every downstream stage already derives height; agent-handler was the only module believing 32 rows. Overseer verification on the merged tree: baseline on master 99bc74c measured firsthand at 4468 passed/3 skipped, merged 4488/3/0 (+20), tsc clean, build clean. Independently re-planted the tile ceiling (448->512): 3 rows red incl. one that discriminates 448 from the old 512, exact assertion 'promise resolved { tiles: 449 } instead of rejecting'; restored clean. Ran a DIFFERENT enumeration frame than the agent's (contract numbers as raw literals, any file type) to test their completeness claim: surfaced 0x7FF in bg-tiles.ts as a candidate duplicate, then dismissed it — 0x7FF is the VDP-wide 11-bit index field used at 17 sites incl. sprites and FG, not a BG-contract number, so leaving it unpinned is correct and pinning it would over-couple. bg-tiles.ts's BG_TILE_BASE_SLOT=1024 IS a genuine second copy and is pinned by drift test rather than imported, deliberately, since bg-tiles.ts is also the classic/S1 loader. Cross-repo sweep for get_bg consumers outside aurora: none read the reply's height field, so making it nullable breaks nothing (only hit is an empyrean status-audit doc listing the method name).

headline: I tried to build a ROM with a moving background band. It doesn't build — and finding out why was the point.
matters: Nobody had ever put an editor-made animated background into an actual ROM, so nobody knew what would happen. I did, and it stops in two places, both on the engine side. First, the engine's tool writes a reference to the animation artwork in a form the assembler won't accept — I found the correct form by looking at a neighbouring file doing the same job, and confirmed it fixes that step. Second, the table that decides how much room each piece of the ROM gets allots this feature exactly two bytes, because two bytes is what the switched-off version takes up; a real band needs about eight thousand. Neither problem is ours and neither could have been found any other way than by trying. Along the way I told you two things that were wrong: that there was spare room nearby (there isn't — what looked like spare room is other artwork, including the very background tiles this whole effort has been about), and that the knock-on effect was contained (it isn't, though it turned out smaller than feared — five pieces shift, not fifteen, because a sound-related address is pinned in hardware and absorbs the rest). The engine lane is doing both fixes as one job. When it lands I run this again and you finally get to watch the background move.
detail: ROADMAP 29-ROM. Isolated worktree of aeon at origin/master 5349bea4; aeon's live tree never touched. Discharges the injector's own :152-159 booking (FORMAT-FAITHFUL BUT NOT BYTE-PROVEN). DEFECT 2: ojz_bg_anim [0x3B270,0x3D29E) overlaps test_mappings [0x3B672,0x3B6A2). NOT the deferred map.toml row (order keys on head-labels, map.toml:73; BgAnim_Table present at :120; the reserved slot at :106-111 names ojz_effects_editor_act1/effects_gen.py). Cause: golden offcanonical_sizes/s4_debug.txt gives BgAnim_Table 0x27e70 -> Map_TestObj 0x27e72, exactly 2 bytes = the stub (u16=0 + Data.empty); real band ~8250. (b) withdrew the cascade prediction on a VACUOUS query -- grepped golden bases for a span taken from build output; golden has zero labels in 0x38000..0x40000, so it could only return 0. Right observable: BgAnim_Table is label 65/80, 15 follow. Cascade settled by aeon reading map.toml:166-176: [[anchor]] dac_banks at=0x48000 hardware-pinned (Z80 SetBank latches LMA), so 5 shift not 15; ~119KB genuine slack in the HeightMaps->Dac_Temp_Blip span. Bounded re-derivation still writes sigil's golden fixture, so the three-lane question is priced down, not withdrawn. Nobody contacts sigil until aeon's parcel lands.

headline: A background parallax scene you build in Aurora now reaches the game running in the emulator.
matters: You asked more than once to see the effects work in the emulator. Tonight the whole chain ran for the first time: five scrolling depth bands were authored in Aurora's Effects panel for the start of act 1, saved, built into the ROM with one Build & Run press, and reloaded into the window you were watching. The engine measurably picked the authored scene, and each band scrolls at exactly the speed typed in. Two engine-side gaps were found and fixed on the way (a missing layout-table row for the first real scene, and the engine preferring its built-in preset over the editor's choice) — both aeon's, both done tonight.

headline: A moving background band built in the editor now runs in the game. It was put into a real ROM, and the animation was watched frame by frame in the emulator.
matters: This is the last piece of the background-effects road. Until tonight a band had never actually run: the editor could save one and the tooling would accept it, but nothing had ever assembled it into a ROM or seen it move. Now the canopy in the jungle level animates, all eight of its frames play in order, and the picture underneath is untouched. You can look at it when you wake — and the same route now works for any band you author.

headline: You can now set how fast a background band moves. Until today every band the editor made ran at exactly one speed.
matters: This was the one gap left by the band you watched animating in the game last night — that band was supposed to move at a chosen speed and the panel had no way to say so, so it took the default. The control warns you that the number runs backwards: a higher setting is a SLOWER band, which is the opposite of what a speed field usually means. Leaving it alone keeps the key out of the file entirely, so a band you never thought about the speed of keeps following the engine's own default instead of being frozen to today's value.

headline: Bands now move inside the editor — and building it turned up that the editor has been showing a different background than the game builds.
matters: You asked to preview how the bands move without going to the emulator. That works now: switch on 'Play bands' and a timer band animates, while a camera-driven band correctly does NOT move on a clock — it moves when you pan, because that is what drives it in the game. With the preview off the viewport costs nothing, exactly as before. The catch is the finding underneath: the picture on the map canvas and the background the ROM is built from are two different files that nothing has ever connected, so on your real project the preview refuses rather than guessing. It says why on screen. Which of the two backgrounds should win is filed as d-11 and is yours to answer.

Verified independently by me: 0/320 by index, 320/320 as a set, decoded past the 2-byte BE header (my first pass was byte-offset and would have falsely contradicted the agent); no library entry matches by index at all; and no aeon tool reads the library, only inject_editor_bg.py reading the override. Agent correctly refused to build the unguarded substitution — every band is licensed by the contract's own prefixIdentity against the DISPLAYED blob, a refused band claims no cells and keeps no clock alive. Also corrected the ruling: the editor pan maps to Camera_X by IDENTITY, not zoom-scaled with its own origin (viewStore.ts:116 divides on the way in; SECTION_PIXEL_SIZE 2048 = aeon's $800); amended in place at the point of the error since item 43 reads that doc next. Incidental fix folded in: MapViewport's ResizeObserver held a drifted near-copy of the draw body passing undefined for object sprites, so a window resize silently downgraded every object preview to a box.

headline: The map now shows you the background the game actually uses — and painting it finally changes the game.
matters: You had two copies of the Oracle Jungle background and they were not the same picture. The editor drew one; the ROM was built from the other. About 1,200 of the map's 4,096 background squares showed different artwork from what the console would show, and nobody could have spotted it by looking. That is now over: the map paints what ships. The moving-band preview you asked for, which refused to run on your real project for exactly this reason, now runs on it and the band moves. The uncomfortable half is what we found on the way in: painting the background in the editor has never reached the game. It edited a picture file the engine does not read, so every background stroke anyone has ever made was thrown away at build time. That is fixed in the same change — a stroke now edits the file the ROM is built from, and you can see it land. And one thing is now refused out loud instead of quietly going wrong: the tile chooser in background mode is showing you the FOREGROUND tiles, which are different art, so about two thirds of the tiles you could pick do not exist in the background at all. Picking one of those used to write a number the console would turn into garbage; it now paints nothing and tells you why. Giving background mode its own tile chooser is written down as the next job rather than bodged in here.

headline: The map now shows the background the game actually builds — and it turned out background painting had never reached the game at all.
matters: This is the call you made today. The editor had been drawing a stale copy of the jungle background while the game was built from a different one, with about 30% of the tiles disagreeing. It now draws the real one, so the band preview works on your actual level instead of refusing — I ran it and the band animates. The unplanned part: because painting wrote to whichever background was on screen, every background tile anyone has ever painted in Aurora went into a file the game does not read. That is now fixed in the same change. One thing is deliberately refused rather than quietly fixed: the tile picker still offers the whole zone tileset while this background only has 320 tiles, so picking one outside that range paints nothing and says so on screen, naming the file and the fix. Booked as its own item because it was equally wrong before today and is not this change's to hide.

headline: The visual band tool you asked for cannot work the way it was specced, and we found that out in an afternoon instead of after building it.
matters: Boxing a region of the background and turning it into an animated band was going to be the other half of the map-preview work. It cannot resolve: the background's tiles are stored across-then-down, while an animated band needs them down-then-across, so a box you draw almost never names a range the engine can animate. At the size both your shipped bands use, it never does. The measurement is banked with the script that produced it, and the shape of the feature is out for a decision rather than being quietly changed into something buildable.
